name: Priya Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Clearline, which sells billing software to small insurance brokers. I'm on the team that keeps the old billing module running, which is Java code older than some of my colleagues. Most days I trace why an invoice came out wrong, fix it carefully, and write up what I did in our wiki. I like it because it's quiet and nobody expects me to invent anything, but I'm slower than the others and I know it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools in that work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No, never. A couple of people on the team paste code into a chatbot, but I don't trust what comes back and I'd rather understand the thing myself. My manager, Gordon, has mentioned it twice in one-to-ones, politely, and I just said I'd look into it. I live with Daniel, my partner, who's an electrician, and he thinks I'm being stubborn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds nice, honestly. That's the one I'd pick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool for some things and leave it at that. I don't post much online, so mostly it'd be at lunch, saying I'm glad we didn't all rush into it. I wouldn't gloat, because half my team uses the stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be a bit worried, because routine work is exactly what I do. Checking invoices and writing up fixes is the kind of thing even a mediocre AI can speed up. If Gordon has to cut one person on our team of five, I'm the slowest, so I'm the one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and try to get faster the normal way, by finishing the Java course I started last year. I'd keep our savings where they are, about four months, and maybe stop the weekly takeaway to add a bit more. I'd probably finally try the AI tool once, just so I can tell Gordon I did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, but I'd still feel watched in the one-to-ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd try the AI tool once so you can tell Gordon. Is that trying it or ticking a box?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ticking a box, if I'm honest. I'd give the AI tool one of our nastier invoice bugs and probably feel pleased when it got it wrong. I know that's not a fair test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Daniel say if you told him you were worried even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say the same thing he always says, that people will always need lights and sockets. He's right about his job. He doesn't really get that mine is all on a screen.

say: AI is a **decent tool** for some things, and I'm glad we didn't rush in.
I wouldn't **gloat**, because half my team uses it already.
think: Checking invoices is exactly the **routine work** even mediocre AI speeds up.
If Gordon cuts one of five, I'm the **slowest**, so it's me.
do: Finish the **Java course** started last year to get faster.
Keep **four months** of savings and drop the weekly takeaway.
Try the AI tool **once** so she can tell Gordon she did.
feel: **Uneasy**, and still feeling **watched** in one-to-ones with Gordon.
S0.quote: I'd give the AI tool one of our nastier invoice bugs and probably feel pleased when it got it wrong. I know that's not a fair test.
fieldNote: She admits her one **AI trial** would be designed to fail.
Even small, routine automation touches her **invoice-checking** work.
Partner's **electrician job** feels safe to him, and he doesn't grasp her screen risk.

steps.text: Keep fixing invoice bugs in Clearline's old billing module
Finish the Java course she started last year
Drop the weekly takeaway to add to savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Coding and checking. That's my whole job description in two words.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it at work in a neutral way, like 'we'll see how it goes'. With friends I'd say it's a shame for people who like doing things properly. I wouldn't pick a side online, because I can see why companies want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Gordon would be told to do more with fewer people, and I'd be in the first group to go. The others would use AI to fix invoice bugs in half the time, and I'd still be reading the code line by line. I can't see a version of this where refusing the tools works out for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd force myself to use the AI tool for a few weeks, with Leon, the colleague I trust, checking how I do it. I'd also start looking at other jobs, probably testing or support roles in bigger firms that might move slower. I'd stop the takeaways and the cinema and try to get to six months of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It feels like being told the exam has changed after I'd learnt the old one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at testing or support roles. Aren't those on the list too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I know that. I'd be looking for anything slower, like a council or a hospital IT team, where change takes years. It's not a great plan, it's just a slower clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if you lost the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My car, probably. I drive to Clearline, but Daniel could drop me places, and the car payment is the biggest thing after rent. We could live on his pay for a while, but not well.

say: We'll **see how it goes**, said in a neutral way at work.
I can see why **companies** want it, so I wouldn't pick a side.
think: Gordon would be told to do more with **fewer people**, and I'd go first.
Refusing the tools **can't work out** for me in this picture.
do: Use the AI tool for **a few weeks** with Leon checking her work.
Look for jobs in **slower places** like council or hospital IT.
Stop takeaways and cinema to reach **six months** saved.
feel: **Anxious**, as if the exam **changed** after she'd learnt the old one.
S1.quote: I'd be looking for anything slower, like a council or a hospital IT team, where change takes years. It's not a great plan, it's just a slower clock.
fieldNote: She is clear-eyed that **refusing AI** fails here, yet still reluctant.
Her escape plan is to find a **slower employer**, not new skills.
The **car payment** is the first thing she'd cut if laid off.

steps.text: Use the AI tool for weeks with Leon checking
Apply for council or hospital IT jobs
Build savings to six months of costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028. That's no time at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to slow it down or at least cushion it, which isn't really me, I'm usually in the middle. At work everyone would be saying the same thing, so I'd just agree. I don't think I'd post, because what would I add?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd lose my job, probably within a year of it arriving, maybe before. Everything I do is on a screen, so the three-year wait for robots means nothing for me. It means a lot for Daniel, though, because his work is hands-on until around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd sell the car and cut our spending to rent, food and bills. I'd ask Daniel if I could work as his electrician's mate, carrying, pulling cable, doing the paperwork for his jobs, because that's hands-on. I'd also apply to the evening electrical course, even though I'd hate starting over at 27.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I picture the HR email and my hands going cold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hate starting over. What would be hardest about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being bad at something in front of people again. I only just stopped feeling like the new girl at Clearline. Being the slow one on a building site would be worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And what if Daniel's work dried up too, as the robots got closer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I don't know. That's 2031 in this picture, and I can't plan that far when 2028 is already this bad. We'd probably move in with his mum for a while.

say: The government needs to **slow it down** or at least cushion it.
I'd mostly **agree** at work, because everyone would be saying it.
think: I'd lose my job **within a year** of it arriving, maybe before.
Daniel's **hands-on** work lasts until about 2031; mine doesn't.
do: Sell the **car** and cut spending to rent, food and bills.
Work as Daniel's **electrician's mate** doing cable and paperwork.
feel: **Alarmed**, picturing the HR email and her hands going **cold**.
S2.quote: I only just stopped feeling like the new girl at Clearline. Being the slow one on a building site would be worse.
fieldNote: She grasps the **robot gap** and pins her plan on Daniel's trade.
Fear of **looking slow** in public weighs on her more than money.
Beyond 2031 she has **no plan** except family support.

steps.text: Sell the car to clear the monthly payment
Cut household spending to rent, food and bills
Join Daniel's jobs as an electrician's mate
Move in with Daniel's mum if both incomes fail

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. That's like the fast one but with some breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for companies and government to plan, and they should. I'd say it without much passion, because I don't think they will. Mostly I'd keep my head down at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have two or three okay years at Clearline before the squeeze. I'd probably still not use the tools much, which means I'd fall behind faster than the others. So the five years is really more like three for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and save hard, aiming for six months by the end of the first year. In year two I'd start the electrical course two evenings a week, so by 2030 I'd be qualified to work with Daniel. I'd keep the car until I actually needed to sell it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier than with 2028. At least I could see the steps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said five years is really three for you. Couldn't you get more by using the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. I just know myself, and I'd keep putting it off until it was obviously too late. Maybe if someone made it part of my job description I'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you and Daniel talk about this at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be practical. My partner Daniel would draw our whole plan on the back of an envelope: two years of me at Clearline, then the course, then I join his electrical business. He'd be more excited than me, because he's always wanted a business partner he trusts.

say: Five years is enough for companies and government to **plan**, and they should.
I'd keep my **head down** at work and not make a fuss.
think: I'd get **two or three** okay years at Clearline before the squeeze.
Avoiding the tools means the five years is **really three**.
do: Save hard to reach **six months** by end of year one.
Start the **electrical course** two evenings a week in year two.
Keep the **car** until it actually has to go.
feel: **Anxious** but steadier, because she can **see the steps**.
S3.quote: My partner Daniel would draw our whole plan on the back of an envelope: two years of me at Clearline, then the course, then I join his electrical business.
fieldNote: She sees her **resistance** shortening her runway and admits it.
Only a **job requirement** would push her to use AI.
Joining **Daniel's business** turns from emergency into a real plan here.

steps.text: Save to six months of costs within a year
Take the electrical course two evenings a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough that I'd probably not think about it much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time and people shouldn't panic. I'd also say the government should use the time sensibly, which is about as political as I get. Nobody at work would be very worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the danger for me is that the tools keep creeping into my job every year before 2036. People like Leon would get better at using them, and I'd stay the same. So I'd be the one let go long before AGI even arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and finish the Java course properly this year. I'd tell myself I'll try the AI tool seriously next year, and I think I'd actually do it, slowly. Daniel and I would probably go ahead with buying a small house, since ten years feels long enough to make some progress on a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in a low, background way. Like a dentist appointment that's months off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be let go before AGI arrives. Is that because of AI or because of you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, honestly. The tools make the gap visible, but the gap is me not wanting to change. I'd like to think ten years would wear that down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the house now, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's the first picture where it doesn't feel reckless. Daniel's work is safe until the late 2030s, and my pay helps with the deposit now. With two years I'd never sign a mortgage.

say: Ten years is **plenty of time**, so people shouldn't panic.
The government should **use the time** sensibly, but nobody at work would be worried.
think: AI tools **creep in** every year, long before 2036.
Colleagues like Leon get better while I **stay the same**, so I'd go first.
do: Finish the **Java course** properly this year.
Try the AI tool **seriously** next year, slowly.
Buy a **small house** with Daniel while both incomes hold.
feel: **Anxious** in a low, background way, like a **dentist appointment** months off.
S4.quote: The tools make the gap visible, but the gap is me not wanting to change.
fieldNote: She blames her own **resistance** more than AI or employers.
Long warning opens a **house purchase** she rules out elsewhere.
Her mood stays **anxious** because the gradual creep hits her early.

steps.text: Finish the Java course this year
Try the AI coding tool seriously next year
Buy a small house with Daniel

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I wouldn't change fast enough and I know it. What would help is a proper paid apprenticeship for adults, not just evening classes. If I could earn a little while I learned Daniel's trade, I'd do it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I'd be sad about software itself. I would, a bit. I'm not brilliant at coding, but I like the quiet of tracing a bug through old code until it finally makes sense.

headlineQuote: I'm not brilliant at coding, but I like the quiet of tracing a bug through old code until it finally makes sense.
portrait: Priya is a **27-year-old** junior developer maintaining an old billing module at Clearline.
She **never uses AI tools**, distrusts them and admits she's the slowest on her team.
Her **centre outlook** keeps her neutral in public and focused on practical steps.
Partner Daniel's **electrician trade** is her fallback in every fast AGI picture.
She stays **anxious or worse** in most pictures because her resistance shortens her runway.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she knows she wouldn't **change** fast enough.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid apprenticeship** for adults so she could earn while learning Daniel's trade.
